clue.text: Wives go wrong, taking left turn

indicators.note: to go wrong is to go astray, so the letters of the word before are thrown out of their order

explanation.surface: Wives misbehave and take a turn to the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go wrong' rearranges WIVES into SWIVE; 'taking' joins on L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: To pivot round on a fixed point is to turn, as a chair on a pin does.

clue.text: Tried extortion from Dr -Grace — run in

indicators.note: the word in tells us the run is placed inside the doctor's initials

parts.note: Dr W. G. Grace, the great Victorian cricketer, was a doctor and is known by his initials WG
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tried to blackmail the cricketing doctor, and a run was involved.
explanation.walkthrough: W. G. Grace was a qualified doctor and England's most famous early cricketer; a run is a cricket score, which feeds the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Money wrung from someone has been extracted by force or pressure, the sense of extortion.

clue.text: Game for the majority '(once) of Frenchmen

definitions.meaning: a card game, the French name of the game also called pontoon or blackjack
the age of majority, coming of age, was formerly twenty-one in France, and the French for twenty-one is the answer

explanation.surface: A game played for the coming of age of young Frenchmen in former times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'majority' here is legal adulthood, not most people; it was formerly reached at twenty-one.
explanation.definitionFit: The card game pontoon takes its name from French twenty-one, the old age of legal adulthood.

clue.text: Find, see and hear a shrew

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see

indicators.note: hear tells us the following word is said aloud and spelt differently

parts.note: Kate is the title shrew of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew

explanation.surface: Track down a small mammal by looking and listening.
explanation.walkthrough: The shrew is not the animal but Shakespeare's Kate; 'hear' turns her name into the sound-alike CATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To pinpoint where something is means to discover it, a synonym.

clue.text: What could make some women drool? A hamburger?

definitions.text: What could make some women drool?
definitions.meaning: slang for a display of muscular, attractive men
read literally, a hamburger is a cake of beef

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a display of muscular male bodies, and literally a patty or cake made of minced beef.

clue.text: Sensational error Odo hadn't somehow taken in

indicators.note: taken in says the word for the error swallows up the anagrammed letters

parts.note: a blunder is an error

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters arrive by some unknown route, so they are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sensational mistake, which Odo somehow failed to absorb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' turns ODOHADNT into OODANDTH, and 'taken in' places that inside BLUNDER, after its BL.
explanation.definitionFit: Melodramatic, lurid stories full of violence are described with this phrase, hence sensational.

clue.text: The East embraces English people, that's right

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so the first word wraps around the others

parts.note: taken as written, the word east
men means people

explanation.surface: The East welcomes English people, and that is as it should be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraces' puts E and MEN inside EAST; 'that's' only links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, a right held over another's land, such as a right of way, has this name.

clue.text: Gripped by huge bird going up, we show fear

indicators.note: being gripped by something means sitting inside it, so the pronoun goes into the bird
in a down clue going up means reading the bird's name from bottom to top

parts.note: the roc is the enormous mythical bird of the Arabian Nights
taken as written

explanation.surface: Seized by a giant bird flying upwards, we are terrified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going up' turns ROC into COR, and 'Gripped by' puts WE inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To crouch or shrink back in terror is to show fear.

clue.text: Change broken set — for this ?

indicators.note: change as a command to alter, so the following letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Swap a broken set of something for this replacement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' rearranges BROKEN SET; read whole, a broken set (paving sett) could be changed for one of these edging blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Edging blocks along a pavement are set stones, so broken sets may be replaced by them.

clue.text: Little dog can back promises with fighting spirit

parts.note: a pug is a small snub-nosed dog

indicators.note: back as in going backwards, so the tin's name reads in reverse

parts.note: taken as written
IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: A small dog backs up its promises with plenty of fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like a verb meaning support, but it turns CAN into NAC.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone combative and eager to quarrel shows fighting spirit, a synonym.

clue.text: Here was a great place for retirement

definitions.text: Here was a great place for retirement

parts.words: Here was a great place for retirement
parts.note: retirement means going to bed, and the Great Bed, an enormous Elizabethan four-poster, is named after the Hertfordshire town where it stood

explanation.walkthrough: The Great Bed of Ware, a huge Elizabethan bed now in the V&A, came from this Hertfordshire town; 'retirement' is going to bed, not leaving work.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hertfordshire town famous for its oversized Great Bed, the place one retired to.

clue.text: I tie knots in the old and nervous

indicators.note: in places the first pieces within the word for the old

parts.note: aged means old, as in the aged, elderly people
to tat is to make tatting, a lace made by tying knots

explanation.surface: I tie myself in knots among the elderly and anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tie knots' is TAT, from tatting lace, not an anagram signal; I and TAT go inside AGED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone flustered and on edge is nervous, a synonym.

clue.text: Doctor got out of bed — on the wrong side ?

definitions.text: Doctor got out of bed — on the wrong side ?

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor
rose means got up from bed

explanation.surface: The doctor got up on the wrong side of the bed this morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting out of bed on the wrong side is the idiom for waking up in a sulky mood, which the whole clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who got out of bed on the wrong side is sullen and gloomy all day.

clue.text: Smooth, useless tyre

definitions.meaning: a punctured tyre, out of air and no use

explanation.definitionFit: Even and level like a calm surface, and also a deflated, punctured tyre.

clue.text: City of Crete lies in ruins

indicators.note: in ruins means wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A city of ancient Crete now lies in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in ruins' rearranges CRETE LIES; 'of' is a link word, and the city is in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral city in the East Midlands of England, an example of a city.

clue.text: This shop's never closed

parts.note: a closed shop is a workplace where every worker must belong to a trade union, so one never closed admits all

explanation.walkthrough: A closed shop is a workplace where union membership is compulsory; the surface suggests a store open all hours.
explanation.definitionFit: A workplace not restricted to trade union members is the opposite of a closed shop.

clue.text: The game of racing

definitions.meaning: a card game in which players stake on cards laid out as horses
the Suffolk town that is the historic home of British horse racing

explanation.definitionFit: A card game, and the Suffolk town known as the headquarters of British horse racing.

clue.text: Taps have running water, that's very certain

parts.note: cocks are taps or valves controlling flow
the Sure is a river flowing through Luxembourg and into the Moselle

explanation.surface: Taps that have running water are reliable.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sure (Sauer) is a European river; 'have' only links COCKS to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Overconfident and arrogantly certain, a strengthened synonym of very certain.

clue.text: Shows the way to deal with the mail

definitions.meaning: a roadside post with pointing arms giving directions, or to mark a route
read as two words, to put a signature on and send letters

explanation.definitionFit: A pointing roadside marker directs travellers; split, it means sign letters and send them.

clue.text: Girl serving Christopher

definitions.meaning: a member of the Women's Royal Naval Service, a woman serving in the navy
Sir Christopher, architect of St Paul's Cathedral

explanation.definitionFit: A woman in the Royal Navy's women's service, and the surname of St Paul's architect Sir Christopher.

clue.text: Sung about hourly

parts.note: C, circa, means about
horal means relating to hours, hourly

explanation.surface: Something sung roughly every hour, like chimes.
explanation.walkthrough: HORAL is a rare word for hourly; C is circa, about.
explanation.definitionFit: Music for a choir is sung, so the adjective describes singing.

clue.text: Withdrawal of protagonist in filmed court action causes comment

indicators.note: withdrawal read as drawing back, so the name is pulled backwards

parts.note: Kramer is the hero of Kramer vs Kramer, a film about a custody court case

explanation.surface: A leading character leaves a courtroom drama, prompting comment.
explanation.walkthrough: Kramer vs Kramer (1979) is a film about a custody case; 'Withdrawal of' reverses KRAMER.
explanation.definitionFit: An observation or remark made aloud is a comment.

clue.text: Do Colorado skiers tremble here like this?

definitions.text: Do Colorado skiers tremble here like this?

parts.words: Do Colorado skiers tremble here like this?
parts.note: a Colorado ski resort shares its name with a tree whose leaves famously quiver in the slightest breeze

explanation.walkthrough: The ski resort in Colorado is named after the quaking tree, whose leaves tremble.
explanation.definitionFit: A Colorado ski resort, and a poplar known for trembling leaves.

clue.text: Big disturbance makes Paul have a convulsion

indicators.note: a convulsion is a violent spasm, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: Something so disturbing it gives Paul a fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have a convulsion' reads as the action, but PAUL HAVE is the anagram fodder and 'a convulsion' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent upheaval of affairs is a big disturbance.

clue.text: A professional baritone's penultimate appearance in "Pinafore "

parts.note: pro is short for professional

indicators.note: penultimate means last but one, so take the letter before the final one of the singer

explanation.surface: A professional baritone's last-but-one appearance in an operetta.
explanation.walkthrough: H.M.S. Pinafore is a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta, but here the pinafore is a garment; 'penultimate' takes N from BARITONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinafore is a sleeveless garment tied over clothes to keep them clean, a synonym.

clue.text: Walk in haste, perhaps

indicators.note: in here means contained within, so the answer lies inside the following words

explanation.surface: Walk quickly, maybe, if you are in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals letters running across 'haste, perhaps', from the end of the first word into the start of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A pace taken on foot is one unit of walking, and to tread is to walk.

clue.text: Lingerie continental articles to pass round

parts.note: un is a French article, a
der is a German article, the
to skirt is to go round the edge of

explanation.surface: Lingerie from the continent, items to be passed around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'continental articles' gives two words: French UN and German DER.
explanation.definitionFit: A petticoat worn beneath a skirt is an item of lingerie, an example.

clue.text: Garden reduced to half your splendour

indicators.note: reduced as in broken down, so the letters are rearranged
half here takes the second half of the following word

explanation.surface: Your garden cut back to half loses its splendour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' rearranges GARDEN into GRANDE; 'half' takes UR, the back half of YOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnificence and impressive splendour are synonyms.

clue.text: Dead, not heartlessly, sleeping

parts.note: late means dead, as in the late king

indicators.note: heartlessly means without its heart, so only the outer letters of the word stay

explanation.surface: Dead, though not cruelly, merely asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' removes O from NOT, leaving NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying dormant, present but inactive, as a sleeping volcano is.
